U.S.-China relations: Avoiding the worst case isn’t good enough
The prevailing conclusion is that the Trump-Xi meeting was ‘a diplomatic nothing burger’

U.S. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump greet Chinese leader Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the White House on Friday.
| REUTERS

By Brad Glosserman

The most common reaction — among U.S. observers — to the recent summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s leader Xi Jinping is a sigh of relief. Fears that Trump would make concessions over Taiwan or U.S. allies in the Asia-Pacific region, like Japan, that damage their interests proved groundless.Instead, the prevailing conclusion is that the meeting was “a diplomatic nothing burger,” in the words of regional analyst James Crabtree, “plenty of pageantry, but no substance.” If “making nice” was the sum of the summit, then it should be considered a success, and not just for having avoided the worst-case outcome. Unfortunately, there may be negative consequences after all.You have to squint to find actual deliverables from the meeting. The two men agreed to extend their trade truce for just two months and enact reciprocal tariff cuts on $60 billion in exports, or $30 billion apiece. Most of those are anticipated to be on agricultural goods.The U.S. readout says the joint U.S.-China Board of Trade, announced in June to manage trade in nonsensitive goods, established a working group that will focus on market-access barriers in agriculture. It also reported that China committed to import 10 million tons of coal annually from the U.S. for two years, while both sides agreed to continue talks regarding U.S. concerns over rare earths and critical mineral shortages. Oh yeah — the U.S. gets two pandas, too.Otherwise, it’s thin gruel. They agreed to work together on artificial intelligence, but they merely committed to set up a dialogue mechanism to exchange views on AI-related risks and benefits. It will meet in November; hopefully humanity will still be around then. They agreed to establish a bilateral communication channel for AI-related incidents that was referred to as a “hotline.” I don’t expect much from this for reasons I laid out recently.The readouts mention geopolitical issues like Iran, North Korea and Russia in general terms, and acknowledged an intent to work together on counternarcotics efforts and at meetings like APEC and the Group of 20. Export controls on semiconductors weren’t mentioned, while Taiwan was only in the Chinese readout, as was the intent to sign a memorandum of understanding on mil-mil crisis communications.Get your facts straight, every dayIn a time of information overload and misinformation, quality journalism is more crucial than ever. Help us get the story right.For a limited time, we’re offering a discounted subscription plan.Unlimited accessUS$30 US$18/moFOREVERsubscribe NOWDrew Thompson, a former Pentagon official who now lives in and opines from Singapore, applauded “a positive tone for the bilateral relationship which is absolutely necessary if any progress is to be made on narrowing differences in the key issues.” He concluded in his Substack that “positive vibes, not much substance is a win-win outcome.”Chinese assessments are strikingly different. A page-one account in People’s Daily called it “an event that will go down in history,” in which “a win-win logic has replaced zero-sum competition” and “demonstrates the new atmosphere and reshaping of the world brought by the Eastern power China as it advances step by step toward great rejuvenation.” The Global Times, the nationalist tabloid, called the results “historic” and “a vision for the two countries to explore the right way for major powers to get along.”Thompson’s right that summits aren’t where detailed discussions occur and their real value is setting the tone for underlings. “Xi Jinping is not a negotiator, he is the penultimate leader who guides the Communist Party.” Summits like this, he wrote, “serve as forcing functions and a hard deadline to prompt the two bureaucracies to work toward outcomes and reach compromises.”I get it, but I don’t know. Trump was all in on the pomp, doing everything he could — red carpet, personal greeting at the airport, flyovers, bonhomie — to impress his “friend,” Xi. (He even reportedly tried to sell Xi U.S. weapons.) Every China expert I know says that personalized approach fundamentally misunderstands the Chinese leader’s mentality and motivations.As Sari Havren, a geopolitical analyst and fellow at the U.K. think tank RUSI, explained on social media, “Xi Jinping is not Donald Trump’s friend. Xi has never addressed Trump as an old friend as he does with Putin.” Another veteran China-watcher sniffed, “Xi doesn’t do friends.”Journalist Josh Rogin has interviewed Trump about this relationship and wrote that “Trump thinks they are friends. He thinks they really like each other. And he thinks that friendship can get all sorts of things for him and for the United States. He thinks that President Xi is not going to attack Taiwan, because he wouldn’t do that to his friend Donald Trump.” Ryan Hass, a China adviser for former President Barack Obama, added on social media that “Xi talks in terms of state-state relations and power. Trump talks in terms of personal chemistry. The contrast is pretty stark.”In addition to missing the point, there is a real danger in framing the relationship in these terms. Nicholas Burns, a former U.S. ambassador to China, warned that Trump “is pulling too many punches. He hasn’t raised Taiwan effectively. ... Chinese support for Iran and for Russia in the Ukraine war. ... We need to be truth-tellers with the Chinese, and I think they will respect us more if we’re stronger at the negotiating table.”Thompson’s “respectful, cordial stalemate” suggests that positions on big issues — most notably Taiwan — are unyielding. Trump said they didn’t talk much about the topic and David Perdue, his ambassador to China, said “nothing has changed. ... we’re not changing the language,” adding that the two sides recognized each other’s position and left it at that.The test will be arms sales to Taiwan, currently on hold to avoid roiling the relationship. With the prospect of another Trump-Xi meeting ever on the horizon, the inclination to continue holding back will be strong.Japan doesn’t have to decipher policy toward Taiwan for hints about potential impacts on its interests. In both summit readouts, there is reference to China-U.S. cooperation during World War II, noting that “China and the United States were allies during World War II and fought side by side to achieve victory.”That statement reflects Beijing’s determination to identify Japan as a former adversary and enlist other countries in the campaign to isolate it diplomatically. This stems from Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s statement last year that a crisis in Taiwan would impact Japan’s national security and justify invocation of its right to exercise collective self-defense.Kenji Minemura, a researcher at the Canon Institute for Global Studies, wrote on X that this means the U.S. government “formally endorsed in writing Xi’s historical perspective” that the two countries “fought together against Japanese militarism,” adding that “this has given a certain degree of success to China’s ‘history war’ aimed at driving a wedge between Japan and the U.S.”Tetsuo Kotani, professor at Meikai University, concurs, noting in an email that this “shows that the cognitive warfare campaign Xi has waged over the past year has paid off.” Japan’s failure to see this coming “suggests communication between Tokyo and Washington is falling short in areas beyond investment and economic security.”All this smacks of a “Yalta 2.0,” in which the U.S. and China “negotiate over Japan’s head,” writes Yasushi Ohara, a public affairs analyst, in Toyo Keizai.Global Times did its best to rub salt in the wound, writing that the U.S.-China convergence on this issue “constitutes a decisive blow to the Japanese government, which is currently seeking to alter the course of history and revive militarism. This is the most important fact of international politics in 2026. ... The U.S. is beginning to acknowledge that it must build a constructive relationship with China. ... Against this backdrop, Japan’s predicament looks especially acute.”In his invaluable Observing Japan Substack, Tobias Harris noted that Takaichi “shrugged off” these concerns, with the prime minister saying that “the U.S. and Japan have strong bonds of affection forged into their postwar reconciliation.” Yeah, but the contrast in the meeting that Takaichi had with Trump in New York on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly and that afforded Xi in Washington is unmistakable. (Harris also alerted me to the Ohara essay noted above.)Yoichiro Sato, professor at Ritsumeikan Asia Pacific University, echoed Takaichi’s line in an email. The summit “produced little but photo opportunities” and, significantly, “Trump did not bargain away arms sales to Taiwan, which put Japan at ease.” Kotani, the professor at Meikai University, countered that “Trump has effectively halted arms sales to Taiwan ... a major win for Xi.”It’s tempting to call this summit a Rorschach test, more indicative of the viewer’s mindset than the meeting itself. It’s clearly indicative of a larger shift in the balance of power between the U.S. and China. But that is part of a more sweeping transformation and the resulting need to better accommodate “the rest.” Last week’s meeting gives us no better sense of what that world looks like.Brad Glosserman, a senior adviser at Pacific Forum, is the author of “Peak Japan.” His latest book, written with David Lee, “Tech-Gemony,” on the geopolitics of high-tech, is out now from Hurst Publishers.
